case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), which prohibits individuals subject to domestic violence civil protective orders from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as interpreted in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8) — federal statute prohibiting firearm possession by persons subject to qualifying domestic violence civil protective orders; Second Amendment to the United States Constitution; and the historical tradition framework established in Bruen (2022)
case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(8) is constitutional because it is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of disarming individuals who pose a credible threat to the physical safety of others, particularly intimate partners and family members, and that the Fifth Circuit erred in striking down the statute by applying Bruen's historical analogue test too rigidly and narrowly. Supporting amici — including domestic violence organizations, public health researchers, medical associations, and prosecutors — further contend that disarming domestic abusers subject to protective orders is firmly grounded in historical surety laws, going-armed laws, and other founding-era traditions, and that upholding the statute is critical to protecting victims of domestic violence and public safety.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Zackey Rahimi argues, and the Fifth Circuit agreed, that the government failed to identify a sufficiently analogous historical tradition of firearm regulation that would justify § 922(g)(8) under the Bruen framework, which requires that modern gun regulations be consistent with the historical tradition of firearm regulation in America at the time of the founding. Rahimi contends that civil protective orders are a modern legal mechanism without a direct historical analogue sufficient to justify a categorical firearms prohibition under the Second Amendment.
key_precedents: New York State Rifle & Pistol Association, Inc. v. Bruen, 597 U.S. 1 (2022) — established the historical tradition test for Second Amendment challenges
District of Columbia v. Heller, 554 U.S. 570 (2008) — recognized an individual right to keep and bear arms but acknowledged the right is not unlimited
McDonald v. City of Chicago, 561 U.S. 742 (2010) — incorporated the Second Amendment against the states
United States v. Rahimi, 61 F.4th 443 (5th Cir. 2023) — the Fifth Circuit decision under review, which struck down § 922(g)(8)
Arizona v. Evans, 514 U.S. 1 (1995) — referenced in amicus briefing regarding the value of lower court percolation on novel constitutional questions
Historical surety laws and going-armed laws from the founding era — cited by amici as analogical historical predecessors to § 922(g)(8)
case_analysis.legal_complexity: Complex — the case sits at the intersection of Second Amendment doctrine, domestic violence law, public health policy, and the proper methodology for applying Bruen's historical analogue framework, requiring the Court to resolve how strictly or flexibly historical analogues must correspond to modern firearm regulations, with significant implications for the constitutionality of a wide range of existing gun control laws beyond § 922(g)(8) alone

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and I find the core reasoning sound: the Fifth Circuit erred by demanding a historical twin rather than a historical analogue, and founding-era surety laws provide sufficient analogical support for § 922(g)(8) as applied to individuals like Rahimi who have received a protective order with an explicit credible-threat finding. Justice Thomas's concurrence in the result is particularly significant — as the author of Bruen, his acknowledgment that surety laws establish adequate historical grounding forecloses the argument that we are departing from Bruen's methodology. My minimalist instincts counsel writing the majority opinion narrowly: we should uphold § 922(g)(8) only as applied to individuals subject to orders containing an explicit credible-threat finding under (C)(i), expressly reserving judgment on (C)(ii) and the broader categorical prohibitions in other § 922(g) subsections, thereby preserving institutional credibility while avoiding unnecessary constitutional pronouncements. Justice Sotomayor's broader framing about real-world consequences, while compelling as a policy matter, should not drive the doctrinal analysis — the historical tradition framework is sufficient to resolve this case without importing consequentialist reasoning that could destabilize Bruen's methodology in future cases.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Having reviewed my colleagues' arguments in round two, I find the conference has converged on the correct analytical framework, and I write to clarify my position as Bruen's author. Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist framing is precisely right — we should confine today's holding to § 922(g)(8)(C)(i)'s explicit credible-threat finding, and I am gratified that colleagues across the ideological spectrum recognize that the Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin was a methodological error under Bruen's own text, which required only 'relevantly similar' analogues. Justice Alito correctly identifies the strongest argument for Rahimi — that surety laws imposed bond requirements rather than outright disarmament — but this distinction fails because the practical burden of surety laws on those who could not post bond was imprisonment, a more severe deprivation than a temporary firearms prohibition, making the 'how' sufficiently analogous under Bruen's framework. I maintain my position that this holding must be understood as strictly narrow: the individualized judicial finding of credible threat under (C)(i) is constitutionally essential, and I continue to harbor serious skepticism about broader categorical disarmament schemes under other § 922(g) subsections that lack such individualized findings, questions today's ruling must expressly reserve.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist approach — we should decide this case narrowly on the (C)(i) credible-threat-finding prong without prejudging harder questions about (C)(ii) or other § 922(g) provisions. Justice Thomas's concurrence in the judgment is notable precisely because even the author of Bruen recognizes that the Fifth Circuit applied that framework too rigidly; if the architect of the historical-twin methodology acknowledges that surety laws provide sufficient analogical support here, that is powerful evidence the Fifth Circuit erred. The strongest argument for Rahimi would be that surety laws merely required bond-posting rather than outright disarmament, but this distinction fails because the practical effect of inability to post surety — imprisonment and loss of liberty — was more burdensome than a temporary firearms prohibition, and Bruen's 'relevantly similar' standard does not demand identical mechanisms. I write to emphasize that today's holding must be understood as narrow: § 922(g)(8) is constitutional as applied to individuals who have received a judicial finding of credible threat with meaningful procedural protections, and we should not be understood as blessing broader categorical disarmament schemes that lack individualized adjudication.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am fully aligned with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and I want to particularly underscore Justice Jackson's point about the asymmetric real-world consequences of the Fifth Circuit's ruling — domestic violence victims, overwhelmingly women, face dramatically elevated homicide risk when their abusers retain firearm access, and a protective order with a credible-threat finding represents exactly the kind of individualized judicial determination that founding-era surety laws contemplated. Justice Thomas's acknowledgment that even under his own Bruen framework the historical analogues are sufficient is particularly significant, because it forecloses any argument that upholding § 922(g)(8) requires abandoning the historical tradition methodology — it simply requires applying it correctly rather than demanding the 'historical twin' the Fifth Circuit erroneously required. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that surety laws imposed bond requirements rather than outright disarmament, but as Justice Gorsuch notes, the burden and justification are relevantly similar — both mechanisms respond to individualized judicial findings of credible threat by restricting the dangerous person's ability to threaten others with arms. The unanimity of this conference reflects not groupthink but the genuine weakness of the Fifth Circuit's cramped reading of Bruen, which would perversely render the historical tradition framework an engine of constitutional invalidation rather than the workable analytical tool Heller and Bruen together envisioned.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist framing — we should decide this case on the narrowest grounds, focusing on § 922(g)(8)(C)(i)'s explicit credible-threat finding rather than reaching broader questions about (C)(ii) or other § 922(g) provisions. Justice Thomas's willingness to join the majority despite authoring Bruen is itself significant: if the framework's architect reads the historical record as supporting this result, the Fifth Circuit's rigid 'historical twin' demand is plainly wrong. The strongest argument for Rahimi — that Bruen demands precise historical matches — collapses under Bruen's own text, which at 142 S. Ct. 2133 explicitly rejected that reading and required only 'relevantly similar' analogues in justification and burden. Surety laws requiring bond-posting or effective disarmament upon a judicial finding of credible threat to specific individuals map directly onto § 922(g)(8)'s mechanism, satisfying Bruen's 'why and how' inquiry without needing a carbon copy from 1791.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Thomas's observation — notable given that he authored Bruen — that the Fifth Circuit applied the historical analogue test too rigidly by demanding near-identical historical twins rather than relevantly similar analogues. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that surety laws imposed bond requirements rather than outright disarmament, creating a meaningful distinction in 'how' the burden operates; but as Justice Barrett correctly identifies, Bruen's framework asks whether the justification and burden are relevantly similar, not identical, and surety laws that effectively disabled arms-carrying through bond forfeiture are sufficiently analogous in burden to § 922(g)(8)'s prohibition. My textualist and originalist methodology compels me to look at what the founding generation actually understood and practiced, and the historical record — surety laws, going-armed laws, and categorical disarmament of those deemed dangerous — demonstrates that the Second Amendment was never understood to protect individuals who posed a judicially-determined credible threat to specific others. I write to emphasize, consistent with Justice Thomas's concurrence, that this holding must remain narrow: the individualized judicial finding of credible threat is constitutionally essential, and broader categorical prohibitions untethered to such findings would require separate historical justification.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist framing — we should uphold § 922(g)(8) on the narrowest grounds, specifically as applied to individuals like Rahimi who received a protective order with an explicit credible-threat finding under (C)(i), without prejudging harder questions about (C)(ii) or other § 922(g) provisions. Justice Thomas's concurrence in the result is particularly significant given that he authored Bruen — his acknowledgment that surety laws provide sufficient analogical support, while insisting on individualized findings and meaningful procedural protections, actually reinforces the institutional point that Bruen's framework, properly applied, does not require historical twins. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that surety laws only temporarily restricted carrying in public rather than imposing a categorical firearms prohibition, but this distinction in mechanism does not undermine the analogical force when the 'why' — protecting identified individuals from credible threats through judicial process — is identical. As an institutionalist, I am also mindful that the Fifth Circuit's approach, if affirmed, would cast doubt on a wide swath of longstanding regulations and damage the Court's credibility by producing results the historical tradition, fairly read, does not compel.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts's minimalist framing — this case is best resolved on the narrowest possible grounds, upholding § 922(g)(8) as applied to Rahimi specifically because the civil protective order included an explicit credible-threat finding under (C)(i), without prejudging harder questions about (C)(ii) or other § 922(g) provisions. Justice Thomas's concurrence-in-judgment posture is instructive: even the author of Bruen acknowledges that the Fifth Circuit applied the historical analogue test too rigidly by demanding near-identical twins rather than relevantly similar analogues in justification and burden. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that surety laws imposed only temporary bond requirements rather than outright disarmament, and that the procedural protections in civil protective order proceedings may be insufficient — but this objection fails because surety laws did effectively disable arms-bearing for those who could not post bond, and § 922(g)(8) itself requires an individualized judicial finding with notice and opportunity to be heard, satisfying the procedural floor the historical tradition implies. I write to emphasize that today's holding is narrow: the 'why and how' of § 922(g)(8)(C)(i) maps onto founding-era surety and going-armed laws with sufficient analogical force, but we should not be understood as blessing every civil disarmament scheme that lacks equivalent procedural safeguards.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I remain firmly in the Petitioner camp, and I find the collective reasoning of my colleagues — particularly Justice Sotomayor's point about the Fifth Circuit's fatal methodological error in demanding a 'historical twin' rather than a 'relevantly similar' analogue — to be fully consonant with my own analysis. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that surety laws merely required bond-posting rather than outright disarmament, and thus don't provide a sufficiently close analogue for a complete firearms prohibition. But as Justice Gorsuch correctly notes, the practical effect of surety laws — requiring individuals to post bond before carrying arms, with imprisonment as the alternative — functioned as a de facto disarmament mechanism for those who could not or would not comply, and the 'why' of both regimes is identical: preventing individuals judicially found to pose a credible threat from using weapons to harm specific others. My background as a public defender makes me especially attentive to procedural fairness, and § 922(g)(8)(C)(i) actually provides more procedural protection than many founding-era categorical disarmament schemes Justice Gorsuch identifies — there is a judicial finding, with notice and opportunity to be heard, before any prohibition attaches, which satisfies both the historical tradition test and basic due process values.

John Roberts.reasoning: The historical record demonstrates that founding-era surety laws and going-armed laws authorized courts to disarm or restrain individuals who posed a credible threat to the physical safety of specific others, even absent a criminal conviction — precisely the mechanism at work in § 922(g)(8)(C)(i), which requires a judicial finding that the subject poses a credible threat to an intimate partner or family member. Under Bruen's historical tradition framework, the government need not identify a 'historical twin' but rather a 'well-established and representative historical analogue,' and the surety laws of the post-Revolutionary period, which required dangerous individuals to post bond or face imprisonment and effective disarmament, satisfy that standard when applied to this narrow category of adjudicated threats. My minimalist instincts counsel deciding this case on the narrowest possible grounds — upholding § 922(g)(8) as applied to individuals like Rahimi, who received a protective order with an explicit credible-threat finding under (C)(i), without prejudging the harder questions raised by § 922(g)(8)(C)(ii) or the broader categorical prohibitions in other subsections of § 922(g). Heller itself acknowledged that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that certain regulations are presumptively lawful, and reversing the Fifth Circuit here preserves both that principle and the institutional credibility of a Court that must demonstrate Bruen's framework does not render all modern gun regulations constitutionally suspect.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: While I authored Bruen and remain committed to its historical tradition framework, the historical record reveals sufficient analogues — particularly founding-era surety laws and going-armed laws — that, properly understood, establish a tradition of disarming individuals who posed credible threats to specific others, even absent criminal conviction. The Fifth Circuit applied Bruen too rigidly by demanding near-identical historical twins rather than analogues that share comparable burden and justification; surety laws did impose prospective firearms disabilities on individuals found dangerous, and § 922(g)(8) operates on a similar individualized-threat-finding basis. Heller itself acknowledged that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that certain categories of dangerous persons may be disarmed consistent with the historical tradition. I write separately to emphasize that this holding is narrow — the government must still demonstrate individualized findings of credible threat, and the civil protective order process must afford meaningful procedural protections — and that I remain skeptical of broader categorical disarmament schemes untethered to the founding-era tradition.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: While Bruen's historical tradition framework demands rigor, it does not require a historical twin — as the Court expressly stated in Bruen itself at 142 S. Ct. 2133. The founding-era surety laws, including those rooted in Blackstone's Commentaries recognizing preventative disarmament upon 'probable suspicion' of future violence, provide sufficient analogical support for § 922(g)(8)'s targeted, individualized disarmament of persons judicially determined to pose a credible threat to intimate partners. The Fifth Circuit erred by demanding a near-identical historical precursor rather than asking whether the modern regulation is 'relevantly similar' in justification and burden to historical analogues — a methodology inconsistent with Bruen's own instructions. Furthermore, Heller itself acknowledged the right is not unlimited and that certain categories of dangerous persons may be disarmed consistent with the Second Amendment, and § 922(g)(8)'s narrow scope — requiring a judicial finding of credible threat before any prohibition attaches — aligns with the historical principle that individualized dangerousness assessments can justify temporary firearms restrictions.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 922(g)(8) is plainly constitutional under any reasonable application of Bruen's historical tradition framework. The founding era's surety laws and going-armed laws collectively establish a robust tradition of disarming individuals who posed credible threats to specific persons or the public — the Fifth Circuit erred fatally by demanding a 'historical twin' rather than identifying the underlying principle, which Bruen itself explicitly rejected in footnote 25. Heller acknowledged the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that 'longstanding' regulations protecting public safety remain presumptively valid; disarming adjudicated domestic abusers subject to civil protective orders — where a court has already made a finding of credible threat — fits squarely within that tradition. Beyond the doctrinal analysis, the real-world stakes demand we not lose sight of what is actually at issue: domestic violence victims, disproportionately women, face dramatically elevated risk of lethal violence when their abusers have access to firearms, and striking down this statute would have devastating consequences for the most vulnerable among us.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Fifth Circuit's rigid demand for a historical twin rather than a historical analogue fundamentally misreads Bruen's methodology. As the research confirms, founding-era surety laws and going-armed laws establish a coherent historical tradition of disarming individuals who posed credible threats to identified persons through civil proceedings — the 'why' behind § 922(g)(8) maps directly onto these historical antecedents even if the precise mechanism differs. Bruen itself acknowledged that modern regulations need not be carbon copies of historical laws, only 'relevantly similar' in justification and burden, and a statute protecting domestic violence victims from individuals a court has found pose a credible physical threat fits comfortably within that tradition. The Fifth Circuit's approach would perversely freeze Second Amendment doctrine at 1791 and render unconstitutional a wide swath of sensible, democratically enacted gun regulations that address modern circumstances the Founders could not have anticipated — a workability disaster that Heller itself warned against by acknowledging the right is not unlimited.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Applying Bruen's historical tradition framework, the founding era provides sufficient analogical support for § 922(g)(8) through surety laws and categorical disarmament statutes that conditioned arms-bearing on individualized judicial findings of threatened violence — precisely what a civil protective order embodies. Surety laws required individuals who posed a credible threat of violence to post bond before carrying arms, and categorical laws disarmed loyalists, the mentally ill, and others deemed dangerous without requiring criminal convictions, demonstrating that the founding generation understood the Second Amendment to permit disarming those who posed a demonstrated threat to others. The Fifth Circuit erred by demanding a historical twin rather than a historical analogue, a methodology Bruen itself rejected — the proper inquiry is whether the modern regulation is 'relevantly similar' to historical predecessors in justification and burden, not whether it is identical in mechanism. Section 922(g)(8) requires an individualized judicial finding that the subject poses a credible threat to an intimate partner's physical safety, which is actually more procedurally protective than many founding-era categorical disarmament schemes, and is therefore consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation as Heller and Bruen together contemplate.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The historical record, properly understood as establishing principles rather than requiring historical twins, demonstrates that the founding era recognized the government's authority to disarm individuals who posed credible threats to others' physical safety — surety laws, going-armed laws, and dangerous-person statutes all reflect this core principle. The Fifth Circuit's methodological error was treating Bruen's historical analogue test as demanding a near-identical historical counterpart rather than asking whether the modern regulation fits within a broader historical tradition, which Bruen itself cautioned against by noting that 'historical analogues need not be a historical twin.' Section 922(g)(8) is narrowly tailored — it applies only to individuals who have had an individualized judicial finding that they pose a credible threat to an intimate partner, which maps closely onto the procedural mechanisms of surety laws that required judicial involvement before disarmament could occur. As an institutionalist, I am also mindful that striking down this statute would cast serious doubt on a wide range of longstanding firearm regulations and undermine the Court's legitimacy by producing a result that the historical tradition, read fairly and practically, does not compel.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen's 'why and how' framework, the government need not identify a historical twin but rather a well-established historical tradition that is relevantly similar in justification and burden. Founding-era surety laws and going-armed laws, while not identical to § 922(g)(8), share the same core principle: individuals who posed a credible, individualized threat to the physical safety of others could be disarmed or required to post bond before any criminal conviction. Section 922(g)(8), as applied to Rahimi, operates on precisely this logic — a civil court made an individualized finding that he posed a credible threat to his intimate partner's physical safety, which maps onto the 'why' of historical surety and going-armed laws with sufficient analogical force. Heller itself acknowledged the right is not unlimited and that 'law-abiding, responsible citizens' are the core constitutional beneficiaries, and a person subject to a protective order with a credible-threat finding falls outside that protected core under any reasonable reading of the historical tradition.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 922(g)(8) is constitutional because it fits comfortably within the Nation's historical tradition of disarming individuals who pose a credible threat to others, as evidenced by founding-era surety laws and going-armed laws that authorized pre-conviction disarmament of dangerous persons upon a judicial finding of threat — precisely the procedural mechanism employed here. The Fifth Circuit applied Bruen's historical analogue test with excessive rigidity, demanding a near-identical historical twin rather than a 'relevantly similar' historical tradition, which Heller itself cautioned against by acknowledging the right is not unlimited and that some regulations are presumptively lawful. As a former public defender, I am acutely aware that the practical consequences of striking down this statute are devastating and asymmetric — domestic violence homicides are disproportionately committed with firearms, and protective orders represent a judicial finding, with due process, that a specific individual poses a credible threat to an intimate partner or family member, satisfying both the procedural fairness and historical tradition requirements Bruen demands. The surety law tradition specifically demonstrates that founding-era governments did not hesitate to restrict firearm access for individuals judicially determined to threaten the safety of specific others, making § 922(g)(8) a modern instantiation of a deeply rooted historical practice.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8), which prohibits individuals subject to domestic violence civil protective orders from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as interpreted in New York State Rifle & Pistol Association v. Bruen.

case_analysis.petitioner_position: The United States argues that § 922(g)(8) is constitutional because it is consistent with the Nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation, as the government has long disarmed individuals who posed a credible threat to the physical safety of others. Amici supporting the petitioner — including domestic violence organizations, public health researchers, medical associations, and prosecutors — further argue that disarming domestic abusers subject to protective orders is essential to preventing intimate partner violence and homicide, and that historical analogues such as surety laws and going-armed laws provide sufficient constitutional grounding under the Bruen framework.

Rahimi contends that under Bruen's text-and-history test, the lack of a precise historical twin for this specific disarmament mechanism renders the statute an impermissible modern regulation with no founding-era counterpart.

John Roberts.reasoning: The conference has reached a remarkable degree of consensus, and I find the core reasoning sound: the Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin fundamentally misread Bruen's analogical framework. Justice Thomas's careful attention to the surety laws — particularly that they authorized imprisonment, a far more severe deprivation than disarmament, through civil or quasi-civil proceedings — reinforces my view that § 922(g)(8) fits comfortably within the historical tradition. As Chief Justice, I would assign the majority opinion with an eye toward the narrowest possible holding: that a statute requiring an individualized judicial finding of credible physical threat, with notice and opportunity to be heard, satisfies the Second Amendment under Bruen — without resolving the constitutionality of other firearm regulations or categorical disarmament schemes. Justice Barrett's point about conducting the historical inquiry at the appropriate level of generality is particularly well-taken and should anchor the opinion's methodology, ensuring we do not inadvertently foreclose future cases involving different procedural predicates.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: After reviewing my colleagues' arguments, I find myself in substantial agreement with the core analytical framework, though I write to emphasize the methodological discipline Bruen demands. Justice Barrett's point about conducting the historical inquiry at the 'appropriate level of generality' is well-taken and aligns with my own view that we need not find a civil protective order mechanism in founding-era law — only the underlying principle that credibly dangerous individuals may be disarmed through civil or quasi-civil proceedings. The surety laws, as Justice Alito correctly identifies, share both the 'why' (preventing credible threatened harm to specific persons) and the 'how' (civil proceeding before a neutral magistrate, without requiring criminal conviction) with § 922(g)(8). I remain cautious, however, about the breadth of today's holding — the statute's constitutionality must remain tethered to cases involving genuine individualized judicial findings of dangerousness, and I would resist any reading that permits disarmament based on mere accusation without meaningful procedural safeguards, as the historical analogues themselves contemplated such protections. The Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin fundamentally misread Bruen's analogical methodology, and I concur that reversal is warranted on these facts.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts' methodological point that Bruen requires only a 'well-established and representative historical analogue, not a historical twin,' and that the Fifth Circuit's demand for a precise procedural counterpart fundamentally misreads our precedent. Justice Thomas raises the most intellectually serious concern from within our coalition — his insistence that the statute's constitutionality must be tethered to cases where a neutral adjudicator has made an individualized finding of dangerousness — but this actually reinforces rather than undermines upholding § 922(g)(8), since the statute on its face requires exactly that kind of particularized judicial finding. The strongest argument for Rahimi would be that founding-era surety laws imposed only temporary bond requirements rather than outright disarmament, but as Justice Kagan correctly notes, those laws could result in imprisonment — a far more severe deprivation — making the lesser remedy of temporary disarmament constitutionally unproblematic under the same historical tradition. I would write separately to emphasize that this holding is narrow: it validates § 922(g)(8) as applied to individuals who have received notice, an opportunity to be heard, and against whom a court has made an explicit credible-threat finding, without prejudging the constitutionality of other disarmament statutes that lack these procedural safeguards.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: I am in full agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and I want to particularly commend Justice Thomas's careful engagement with the surety law tradition — even his more cautious framing ultimately confirms that founding-era law permitted pre-criminal disarmament through civil proceedings upon a finding of credible threat, which is precisely what § 922(g)(8) requires. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that modern civil protective order proceedings lack a precise founding-era procedural counterpart, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, Bruen instructs us to reason at the appropriate level of generality — the underlying principle of neutralizing adjudicated individual threats, not the specific procedural mechanism, is the relevant historical anchor. The Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin is not only methodologically wrong under Bruen's own text, but would produce the perverse result Justice Kagan identifies: the government could imprison Rahimi but could not temporarily disarm him, a constitutional regime that defies coherence. Most fundamentally, the real-world stakes — domestic violence victims facing dramatically elevated homicide risk when abusers retain firearms — reinforce that the historical tradition and sound constitutional governance both point unmistakably toward upholding this statute.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, which itself is telling about the strength of the historical record here. Justice Thomas's careful attention to the surety laws — particularly his citation of the 1836 Massachusetts statute and Blackstone's treatment of pre-criminal disarmament — reinforces my view that the founding era recognized a principle of targeted, individualized disarmament based on credible threat findings, not merely categorical class-based restrictions. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that § 922(g)(8) lacks a sufficiently precise procedural analogue because founding-era surety laws operated through different mechanisms and imposed different remedies, but as Justice Barrett correctly notes, Bruen instructs us to conduct the historical inquiry at the appropriate level of generality — the relevant principle is whether the government may disarm individuals adjudged dangerous to specific persons, not whether the precise procedural vehicle matches. The Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin would, as Justice Kavanaugh observes, produce a constitutionally unworkable regime that the historical tradition framework was never designed to mandate, and the statute's procedural safeguards — notice, opportunity to be heard, and a judicial finding of credible threat — actually make it more protective of individual rights than many founding-era mechanisms.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Justice Thomas's careful insistence that the historical grounding must be rigorous and that the statute's constitutionality is not unlimited — the key is that a neutral adjudicator must make an individualized finding of dangerousness, which § 922(g)(8) requires. The strongest argument from Rahimi's position would be that surety laws never actually dispossessed firearms but merely required bond-posting, creating a meaningful procedural gap with § 922(g)(8)'s outright prohibition. However, as Justice Kagan correctly notes, surety laws authorized imprisonment for failure to post bond — a far more severe deprivation than temporary disarmament — which demonstrates that founding-era practice accepted serious liberty deprivations based on civil dangerousness findings, making the lesser remedy of disarmament constitutionally supportable. My textualist and originalist methodology leads me to the same destination as my colleagues: the Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin misreads Bruen's own instruction that analogues, not twins, are required, and the surety law tradition provides the necessary analogical foundation for upholding this narrowly tailored statute.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with Chief Justice Roberts' institutionalist framing and Justice Barrett's methodological point about conducting the historical inquiry at the appropriate level of generality. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that § 922(g)(8) lacks a sufficiently precise historical analogue because civil protective orders are a modern invention — but as Justice Thomas acknowledges even while joining our side, the surety laws permitted pre-criminal disarmament through civil or quasi-civil proceedings upon a finding of threatened breach of peace, which is the relevant analogical principle, not the specific procedural mechanism. Bruen's instruction that we seek a 'historical analogue, not a historical twin' forecloses the Fifth Circuit's demand for a precise procedural counterpart, and the combination of surety laws, going-armed statutes, and Heller's own recognition of presumptively lawful regulations disarming dangerous individuals provides ample historical grounding. I would write narrowly, as Roberts suggests, to hold only that this statute — with its procedural safeguards and individualized judicial finding of credible threat — survives Second Amendment scrutiny, preserving flexibility for harder cases involving less procedurally robust disarmament mechanisms.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: I find myself in substantial agreement with my colleagues across the ideological spectrum, and Justice Thomas's careful attention to the procedural grounding of historical surety laws actually strengthens rather than undermines my position — his observation that surety laws permitted imprisonment based on civil proceedings before a justice of the peace, a far more severe deprivation than firearm dispossession, confirms that the founding generation accepted significant liberty restrictions on individuals adjudged dangerous without requiring criminal conviction. The strongest argument for Respondent would be that § 922(g)(8) lacks a sufficiently precise historical analogue because civil protective orders are a modern invention, but as I emphasized in my Bruen concurrence, the historical inquiry must be conducted at the appropriate level of generality — we ask whether the *principle* of temporarily disarming credibly dangerous individuals through judicial process is historically grounded, not whether the precise procedural mechanism existed in 1791. Justice Kagan's point about the absurdity of a constitutional regime permitting imprisonment but not disarmament of a threatening individual further illustrates why the Fifth Circuit's demand for a historical twin produces results inconsistent with the underlying logic of Bruen itself. The statute's narrow scope — requiring an individualized judicial finding of credible threat with notice and opportunity to be heard — places it squarely within the historical tradition, and Rahimi's facial challenge fails on these facts.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I remain firmly in the Petitioner camp and find myself in strong agreement with Justice Sotomayor's comprehensive analysis, particularly her observation that the Fifth Circuit's methodological error — demanding a historical twin rather than a relevantly similar analogue — is the central flaw requiring correction. Justice Thomas's concurring position is notable because even he, as Bruen's author, acknowledges that surety laws permitting pre-criminal disarmament through civil proceedings upon a finding of threatened breach of peace provide sufficient historical grounding, which significantly undermines any respondent argument that the historical record is too thin. My background as a public defender reinforces rather than complicates this analysis: I have seen both the devastating consequences of domestic violence and the importance of procedural fairness, and § 922(g)(8) satisfies both concerns by requiring actual notice, an opportunity to be heard, and an individualized judicial finding of credible threat before disarmament occurs. The strongest counterargument — that modern civil protective order proceedings lack a precise founding-era procedural analog — fails because Bruen itself explicitly warned against demanding anachronistic specificity, and the underlying regulatory principle of neutralizing adjudicated individual threats to specific persons is robustly supported by the historical record.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under Bruen's text-and-history framework, the government need only identify a 'well-established and representative historical analogue, not a historical twin,' and the historical record amply demonstrates that founding-era and 19th-century legislatures consistently disarmed individuals deemed dangerous or threatening to public safety — through surety laws, going-armed statutes, and disarmament of loyalists and others posing credible threats. Section 922(g)(8) fits comfortably within this tradition because it targets only individuals who have been adjudicated, through a civil proceeding with notice and opportunity to be heard, as posing a credible threat to an intimate partner's physical safety — precisely the category of dangerous persons that historical practice authorized legislatures to disarm. Consistent with my preference for narrow rulings, I would hold only that this specific statute, with its procedural safeguards and credible-threat finding, survives Second Amendment scrutiny, without broadly resolving the constitutionality of other firearm regulations. The Fifth Circuit's demand for a precise historical twin fundamentally misread Bruen and would destabilize a wide range of longstanding, legitimate firearm regulations in a manner that undermines both institutional legitimacy and sound constitutional governance.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: While I write separately to emphasize that Bruen's framework demands rigorous historical grounding and I harbor serious reservations about whether modern civil protective order proceedings map cleanly onto founding-era mechanisms, the historical record does reveal a consistent tradition of disarming individuals who posed a credible, demonstrated threat to the physical safety of others — without requiring a criminal conviction as a predicate. The surety laws documented in Blackstone, incorporated into colonial and early state law, and codified in statutes such as the 1836 Massachusetts Revised Statutes ch. 134 § 16, permitted pre-criminal disarmament upon a finding of threatened breach of peace, and critically, could result in imprisonment — a far more severe deprivation than mere firearm dispossession — based on civil or quasi-civil proceedings before a justice of the peace. Under Bruen's instruction that the government need only identify a 'historical analogue, not a historical twin,' 597 U.S. at 2133, these surety and going-armed statutes, taken together with the broader founding-era principle that dangerousness to specific individuals could justify arms restrictions, provide sufficient constitutional grounding for § 922(g)(8) as applied to individuals subject to protective orders containing explicit judicial findings of credible physical threat. I would nonetheless caution that the statute's constitutionality is not unlimited — its application must be tethered to cases where a neutral adjudicator has made an individualized finding of dangerousness, consistent with the procedural protections the historical analogues themselves contemplated.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Under Bruen's text-and-history framework, the government need not produce a 'historical twin' but rather demonstrate that § 922(g)(8) is 'relevantly similar' to historical analogues in both 'why' and 'how' it burdens the Second Amendment right. The founding-era surety laws provide sufficient analogical grounding: they operated through civil proceedings without requiring criminal conviction, targeted identified individuals who posed a credible threat to specific persons, and authorized temporary disarmament as a preventive measure — precisely the mechanics and justification underlying § 922(g)(8). Rahimi's demand for a precise historical counterpart misreads Bruen, which explicitly acknowledged that modern regulations need not mirror historical ones with 'a dead ringer' but must instead fit within a broader tradition of disarming those who pose a demonstrated threat to others. Heller itself recognized that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that the government may disarm individuals who present a credible danger, and the historical record of surety laws, going-armed statutes, and the broader tradition of preventive disarmament of dangerous persons collectively satisfy the Bruen standard as applied to domestic violence protective orders that afford notice and an opportunity to be heard.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Section 922(g)(8) is plainly constitutional under Bruen's analogical framework because the Nation's historical tradition includes surety laws and 'going armed' statutes that disarmed individuals who posed credible threats to identifiable persons — precisely the 'how' and 'why' that Bruen demands we compare. The Fifth Circuit committed a fundamental methodological error by demanding a historical 'twin' rather than a 'relevantly similar' analogue, a standard Bruen itself explicitly rejected. The statute's procedural safeguards — requiring actual notice and an opportunity to be heard before the protective order issues, per 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(8) — further distinguish this from arbitrary disarmament, grounding it in due process and making it analogous to founding-era judicial mechanisms for restraining dangerous individuals. Beyond the historical analysis, the real-world stakes demand we not lose sight of what is at issue: domestic violence victims, overwhelmingly women, face dramatically elevated homicide risk when their abusers have access to firearms, and a constitutional interpretation that strips Congress of the power to address this documented lethal threat would be both historically unfounded and catastrophically harmful to the most vulnerable among us.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Under Bruen's framework, the government need not produce a 'historical twin' but rather demonstrate that § 922(g)(8) is 'relevantly similar' to historical analogues in both justification and burden — and the surety laws, going-armed statutes, and Statute of Northampton collectively establish a robust founding-era tradition of disarming individuals who posed credible threats to specific persons' physical safety. The surety laws in particular — which allowed magistrates to compel bonds or imprisonment from individuals credibly accused of threatening to breach the peace — share the same core principle as § 922(g)(8): targeted, individualized disarmament based on a judicial finding of threatened harm, not a categorical ban on an entire class. The Fifth Circuit's demand for a precise procedural analogue — a civil protective order mechanism — imposes an anachronistic specificity that Bruen itself cautioned against, since founding-era legislatures could not have anticipated the modern civil protective order system while nonetheless sharing the underlying regulatory principle of neutralizing credible individual threats. As a pragmatic matter, striking down § 922(g)(8) would produce an unworkable constitutional regime where the government can imprison a threatening individual but cannot temporarily disarm them pending a civil proceeding — a result that defies both statutory coherence and common sense.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Under Bruen's text-and-history framework, the government need not produce a 'historical twin' but rather demonstrate that § 922(g)(8) is consistent with the broader historical tradition of disarming individuals who pose a credible threat to others. The historical record reveals that founding-era surety laws, going-armed statutes, and the longstanding principle that legislatures may disarm those who are not 'peaceable' or 'law-abiding' provide sufficient analogical support — surety laws in particular conditioned arms-bearing on posting bond when a complainant demonstrated reasonable fear of violence, which is functionally analogous to a civil protective order predicated on a judicial finding of threatened harm. Critically, Heller itself acknowledged that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that 'longstanding' regulations disarming dangerous individuals are presumptively lawful; a statute targeting persons subject to judicial findings of credible physical threat fits comfortably within that tradition. Rahimi's demand for a precise procedural twin — a civil rather than criminal disarmament mechanism — elevates form over the substantive historical principle that dangerous individuals may be temporarily disarmed, which is the relevant inquiry Bruen actually requires.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: The historical record demonstrates a longstanding tradition of disarming individuals who pose a credible threat to others, which is precisely what § 922(g)(8) does. Surety laws from the founding era and 19th century — including Massachusetts' 1836 statute requiring bond from those creating 'reasonable cause to fear an injury or breach of the peace' — establish that legislatures have long conditioned firearm rights on responsible, peaceable conduct, even through civil rather than criminal mechanisms. Bruen does not require a 'historical twin' but rather a 'historical analogue,' and the principle underlying § 922(g)(8) — that those adjudicated as posing a credible physical threat to identifiable persons may be temporarily disarmed — is well-grounded in that tradition. As an institutionalist, I am also mindful that the Fifth Circuit's rigid application of Bruen would produce an unworkable and socially destabilizing result that the historical tradition framework was never intended to mandate, and that Heller itself recognized the government's authority to impose presumptively lawful regulations disarming dangerous individuals.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Under Bruen's text-and-history framework, the government need not produce a 'historical twin' but rather demonstrate that § 922(g)(8) is 'relevantly similar' to historical analogues in both burden and justification. The founding era's surety laws and going-armed statutes establish a robust tradition of temporarily disarming individuals who posed a credible, particularized threat to the physical safety of others — precisely the predicate that § 922(g)(8)(C)(i) requires through a judicial finding of credible threat. As I emphasized in my Bruen concurrence, the historical inquiry must be conducted at the appropriate level of generality, and the principle underlying these historical laws — that the government may disarm those adjudged dangerous to specific persons pending resolution of that danger — maps directly onto the statute's narrow, procedurally-grounded disarmament mechanism. Rahimi's facial challenge fails on these facts because the protective order here satisfied the most demanding subsection of § 922(g)(8), and the historical record sufficiently supports disarmament conditioned on a judicial finding of specific dangerousness, even absent a criminal conviction.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Section 922(g)(8) is constitutional under Bruen's analogical reasoning framework because the Nation's historical tradition of disarming individuals who posed credible threats to public safety — evidenced by surety laws, going-armed statutes, and Revolutionary-era disarmament of dangerous persons — provides sufficient analogical grounding. The Fifth Circuit committed a fundamental analytical error by demanding a precise historical 'twin' rather than applying Bruen's instruction to identify 'relevantly similar' historical regulations, improperly collapsing the 'how' and 'why' inquiries into a single categorical demand. As a former public defender who has witnessed the devastating practical consequences of intimate partner violence, I am acutely aware that the historical tradition of disarming those who pose credible, adjudicated threats to specific individuals' safety — confirmed through civil proceedings with due process protections — is precisely the kind of enduring principle Bruen's framework was designed to accommodate. Heller itself recognized that the Second Amendment right is not unlimited and that longstanding prohibitions targeting dangerous individuals remain presumptively lawful, and § 922(g)(8)'s requirement of a judicial finding of credible threat satisfies both historical tradition and procedural fairness.
